section_summary: This section documents the organization, personnel rosters, administrative functions, and financial expenditures of the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Gaimusho) and its worldwide diplomatic and consular posts between July 1934 and June 1935. It features detailed reports from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and comprehensive comparative analyses by the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs evaluating staffing levels, salary scales, living quarters, automobiles, and representation allowances between the American and Japanese foreign services. Additionally, the records include correspondence with Professor Kenneth Colegrove concerning his scholarly chapter on the Gaimusho, press reports on Japanese diplomatic expansion and budget limitations, and intelligence studies assessing Japanese governmental and military representation across the United States.

subfiles.about: Transmittal of comprehensive personnel rosters for the Japanese Foreign Office and diplomatic missions and consulates worldwide as of June 1, 1934.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits three comprehensive enclosures detailing the personnel of the Japanese foreign affairs establishment compiled as of June 1, 1934. Enclosure 1 lists all internal officials of the Foreign Office in Tokyo across the minister's secretariat, divisions, and bureaus. Enclosure 2 provides a complete roster of chiefs of mission, counselors, secretaries, and attachés assigned to Japanese embassies and legations globally. Enclosure 3 details consular officers, including consul generals, consuls, vice consuls, and consular police inspectors, stationed at posts throughout Asia, Europe, the Americas, Africa, and Australasia.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 877 from Joseph C. Grew, with Lists of Foreign Office, Diplomatic, and Consular Officials

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Tokyo Embassy despatches on the structure and budget of the Japanese Foreign Office to Under Secretary William Phillips.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, forwards two despatches from the Tokyo Embassy concerning the organization and operating costs of the Japanese Foreign Office to Under Secretary William Phillips. Hornbeck notes that the material will be of significant interest and asks that the documents be returned directly to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs for further consideration.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to William Phillips regarding Foreign Office Organization and Budget

subfiles.about: State Department analysis of the structural reorganization of the Japanese Foreign Office and its diplomatic policy implications.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluates the organizational changes in the Japanese Foreign Office reported by the Tokyo Embassy. It highlights the transformation of the Asia Bureau into an independent Eastern Asia Bureau focused on China and protection cases, and the reorientation of the European and Asiatic Bureau toward Soviet relations at the expense of traditional ties with Britain, France, and the League of Nations. It also emphasizes the elevation of relations with the United States to an independent Bureau of American Affairs, concluding that these structural revisions strikingly illustrate the recent reorientation of Japan's foreign policies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Reorganization of the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Detailed report on the reorganization, jurisdictional functions, domestic prestige, and budgetary constraints of the Japanese Foreign Office under Koki Hirota.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on the reorganization of the Japanese Foreign Office, analyzing its diminished prestige and influence in the wake of the Manchurian crisis, League of Nations withdrawal, and military encroachment on civilian foreign policymaking. He examines the Gaimusho's severe budgetary limitations compared to the armed services, public criticism of its diplomatic corps, and Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's efforts to establish a conciliatory foreign policy and improve commercial efficiency through departmental restructuring. An accompanying enclosure provides a detailed outline of the jurisdictional responsibilities of every bureau and section under Imperial Ordinance as reorganized in June 1934.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 878 from Joseph C. Grew on Foreign Office Organization, Prestige, and Functions

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Eugene H. Dooman's comparative study on the personnel, structure, and expenditures of the American and Japanese Foreign Services.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck submits a comparative study prepared by Eugene H. Dooman to Assistant Secretary Wilbur J. Carr, suggesting it also be brought to the attention of Under Secretary Phillips and Secretary Hull. Hornbeck underscores that the underlying Tokyo despatches show the Japanese Government considers relations with the United States to be of paramount importance and is deliberately expanding its administrative machinery to manage those relations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Wilbur J. Carr regarding Comparative Study of Foreign Services

subfiles.about: Comprehensive comparative study of appropriations, personnel numbers, salary schedules, and representation allowances in the American and Japanese Foreign Services.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman presents an extensive analytical comparison of the organization, staff distribution, budgets, salaries, and perquisites of the American and Japanese foreign services. While Japanese base civil service salaries are exceptionally low, officers stationed abroad receive substantial representation allowances, family allowances, furnished official quarters, automobiles, and access to a Yen 2,500,000 secret fund, making their effective financial compensation considerably higher than that of American officers. Attached statistical schedules detail basic salary scales, representation allowances across global posts, and side-by-side cost comparisons for ambassadors, ministers, consuls general, and consuls in major world capitals.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Comparative Appropriations, Salaries, and Allowances of the American and Japanese Foreign Services

subfiles.about: Instruction directing the American Embassy in Tokyo to submit annual revisions of personnel and seniority lists of the Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State William Phillips refers to Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 877 of July 4, 1934, and directs the mission to submit updated revisions of the Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service rosters upon receipt and at least annually thereafter. Phillips notes that while general personnel lists are readily obtainable from the Gaimusho, the confidential seniority list may be secured through direct request to the Chief of the Bureau of American Affairs.
subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo regarding Annual Personnel Lists
subfiles.to: American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Informal inquiry requesting data on the staff size and personnel assigned to relations with the United States in the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck writes informally to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew asking for comparative data on the personnel assigned to American affairs in the Japanese Foreign Office. Specifically, he requests information on the number of officers and clerks employed in the Bureau of American Affairs, particularly its First Section handling North America, and how many officials across the ministry devote the whole or major portion of their time to relations with the United States.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Joseph C. Grew regarding American Bureau Personnel

subfiles.about: Submission of a draft academic chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office for State Department review, accompanied by manuscript excerpts.
subfiles.summary: Professor Kenneth Colegrove of Northwestern University transmits a draft chapter entitled 'Japanese Foreign Office' from his forthcoming book on Japanese foreign policy to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, requesting that State Department experts inspect the text for errors or misstatements. The accompanying manuscript excerpts examine press relations and the Hikaye Shitsu, the Cultural Relations Board, telegraph message interception and codebreaking by the Denshin-ka, Meiji-era personnel recruitment, competitive civil service examinations under the Yamagata ordinances, overseas allowances, and the general efficiency of Japan's career foreign service. The subfile includes duplicate carbon pages of the manuscript and editorial review markings.
subfiles.title: Letter from Kenneth Colegrove with Draft Chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Acknowledgment of Professor Kenneth Colegrove's manuscript chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Professor Kenneth Colegrove's letter of April 2 and his draft chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office. Hornbeck writes that he has read the chapter, that it is currently being reviewed by a divisional associate, and that it will be returned promptly with any constructive comments.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Kenneth Colegrove acknowledging Draft Chapter

subfiles.about: Return of Professor Kenneth Colegrove's draft chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office with suggested editorial and factual changes.
subfiles.summary: Writing in Stanley Hornbeck's absence, Acting Chief Maxwell M. Hamilton returns Kenneth Colegrove's draft chapter on the Japanese Foreign Office. Hamilton notes that divisional officers thoroughly reviewed the text, found it informative and interesting, and enclosed a few brief notes containing suggested factual corrections.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Kenneth Colegrove returning Draft Chapter with Suggestions

subfiles.about: Transmittal of staffing data on the Gaimusho's Bureau of American Affairs obtained by Edwin L. Neville from Bureau Chief Kensuke Horinouchi.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew responds to Stanley Hornbeck's inquiry of March 15, forwarding personnel data obtained on April 1 by Embassy Counselor Edwin L. Neville from Kensuke Horinouchi, Chief of the Foreign Office's America Bureau. The enclosed report inventories the personnel in the First Section (United States, Philippines, Canada), Second Section (Central and South America), and Third Section (Passports), itemizing the numbers of section chiefs, secretaries, clerks, extra clerks, typists, and office boys.
subfiles.title: Letter from Joseph C. Grew to Stanley K. Hornbeck enclosing Personnel Report on the America Bureau

subfiles.about: Newspaper report on Japanese Foreign Office personnel shortages, diplomatic expansion needs, and Finance Ministry budget cuts.
subfiles.summary: A news report in The Japan Advertiser details statements by Shinrokuro Hidaka, Chief of the Personnel Department of the Foreign Office, emphasizing that Japan's rapid global commercial expansion has overwhelmed existing diplomatic and consular facilities. Hidaka outlines plans approved by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota to establish new legations in Ethiopia and Egypt, consulates in Delhi and Morocco, and expanded staffs throughout Latin America and the Baltic states, while expressing frustration that the Finance Ministry severely slashed these proposed appropriations before the Diet session.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Article on Foreign Office Staff and Budget Deficits in The Japan Advertiser

subfiles.about: Comparative analysis of diplomatic and consular agencies, personnel, facilities, representation allowances, and annual expenditures maintained by Japan in the U.S. versus the U.S. in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum assesses the administrative machinery and expenditures of Japan in the United States compared to American establishments in Japan. While both nations deploy a similar number of career officers (32 Japanese in the U.S. versus 26 Americans in Japan), Japanese personnel enjoy far more generous representation allowances, official automobiles, and free residential quarters. Factoring in Japan's Yen 2,500,000 Foreign Office secret fund used to finance American advisers and propagandists, Japan spends over $100,000 more annually on its establishments in the United States than the United States expends in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Comparative Facilities and Expenditures of Japanese and American Diplomatic Establishments

subfiles.about: Detailed comparative study evaluating diplomatic, consular, commercial, military, and semi-governmental agencies maintained by Japan and the United States for mutual relations.
subfiles.summary: This extensive study examines the administrative and institutional machinery dedicated to bilateral relations by the Japanese Foreign Office and the U.S. Department of State. It outlines the composition of the Gaimusho's American and Commercial Bureaus, inventories all Japanese diplomatic missions and regular and honorary consulates throughout the United States and Hawaii, and contrasts diplomatic remuneration, automobiles, and embassy properties. It also details non-diplomatic Japanese governmental and semi-official missions in the United States—including the Army and Navy attachés, language officers, naval supply office, Finance Ministry agents, Government Railways, Taiwan Government General, and the South Manchuria Railway—noting that the text continues into following pages.
subfiles.title: Study of Japanese and American Agencies for the Conduct of Mutual Relations
